title: Hattie and Peaches Find the Chimes
markdown:
Once upon a time, in an orchard bathed in the softest golden light, there lived a hedgehog named Hattie and a pony named Peaches.

Hattie’s prickles were not sharp. They were like the softest moss on an old stone, a gentle touch for fallen leaves. Every day her heart kept time with the rustle, rustle, rustle of those leaves on the breeze. Peaches had a coat the colour of ripe peaches, warm and soft, and a quiet strength like a hug you could lean on. She cherished the hummm of the wind in her long mane. They were the very best of friends. Their days had a rhythm: the pad of Hattie’s tiny paws, the thud of Peaches’s hooves on earth.

Every day they explored among apple trees and berry bushes. They knew the orchard’s whispers, the wind’s usual song, the soft buzz of bees in blossom. It was a tranquil routine, full of familiar quiet.

Until one day a sound unlike any other floated through. Not rustle. Not hummm. Music. A clear tinkling melody, sweet as the first honey a bee ever made. Delicate. Lovely. It made their hearts feel light and curious.

“Let’s go, Peaches,” squeaked Hattie, fuzzy prickles twitching.

Peaches nodded, eyes sparkling. They set off, paws and hooves soft on the grass, following the tinkling that danced just ahead.

Because of that the wind turned playful. It blew the song this way, then that, as if the orchard were playing hide-and-seek. When the sound hid in a dense patch of tickly bushes, Hattie nudged through, pink nose busy, mossy prickles sliding where sharper ones would have snagged. Leaves caught on her back and then let go. Peaches picked her way over moss and twigs, every hoof sure, stopping when a bramble asked her to.

They came out sneezing blossom. The tinkling had moved.

“Listen,” Peaches whinnied, gentle. “Near the big rosebush.”

They went to the rosebush. Bees were already there, doing important bee work. The chimes seemed to laugh from the other side of the petals, then slip away. Hattie circled the roots. Peaches stretched her neck over the top. No crystal. Only roses, and a snail taking the long way round a stem.

Hattie tilted her head. “Now it sounds closer by the old stone wall.”

The wall was warm from the day’s gold. Lichen made pale maps. They walked its length, Hattie close to the stones, Peaches listening above. The song ran along the wall like a trickle, then hopped off into deeper orchard. They called to each other, a back-and-forth of almost, and the almost kept moving.

Because of that they learned to listen closer. They huddled. Hattie pointed her nose toward the sweetest notes, whole body quivering. Peaches offered a warm flank to lean on while they pondered, a silent agreement not to rush the wind. The music led them into a part of the orchard they had not yet mapped, a secluded nook where sunbeams made tiny golden pools on the grass. Apple smell. Cool shade. Ting, ting, tinkle. They smiled so wide their whiskers — Hattie’s, at least — twitched. The air itself seemed to hum.

Until finally they stepped into a small sun-dappled clearing that seemed to hold its breath. From the slender branches of a weeping willow hung the most beautiful wind chimes they had ever seen: crystal, like captured raindrops, like tiny pieces of frozen moonlight. The wind kissed them, and they sang. Joy in tinkles. Bell-like tones. Hattie, small and nimble, got close. She felt the vibration in the air, smelled faint willow blossom, saw tiny rainbows appear and vanish as the crystal caught the shifting light. A fallen apple lay in the grass, ignored, because the song was better than fruit. Peaches, being taller, nudged the lowest branch with her soft nose. The chimes answered with their most resonant tune, a melody that wrapped around them like a warm blanket.

They did not snatch the song. They stood. Hattie leaned on Peaches’s leg. Peaches lowered her head until her mane mixed with willow-shadow. They listened until the wind rested, and then until it began again.

Ever since then Hattie and Peaches often return to that willow clearing. The orchard still rustles. Peaches’s mane still hums. Only now, when the wind is just right, they know where the extra sweetness lives, and they go, quietly, to hear it together.
